3. Bryopsida (Mosses) The name bryopsida comes from the Greek word ‘bryon’ which means moss. The main characteristics features are given below:

i. The plant body is gametophyte and is differentiated into spirally arranged leaves, axis and rhizoids. ii. Rhizoids are multicellular, branched and have oblique septa. iii. Sex organs are formed at apical portion of stem. iv. The sporophyte is differentiated into foot, seta and capsule. v. Sporophyte is parasite on gametophyte. vi. The columella is present in the capsule and capsule contains ring of teeth like structure known as periostome. vii. Spores germinate to produce protonema stage and then to gametophytic plant body. Examples: Polytrichum, Funaria, Sphagnum, etc.

Position : Plantae : Bryophyta : Hepaticopsida : Marchantiales : Marchantiaceae : Marchantia
Occurrence The thalli of Marchantia commonly grow upon moist, cool and shady places, generally found on soil, rocks, walls, log of wood, trunk of trees and near the bank of rivers and streams.

Plant body The plant body of Marchantia is gametophytic thallus. The thallus is prostate, dichotomously branched and dorsoventral. The thallus is dark green in colour and consists of distinct mid rib. The apex of each thallus has apical notch in which growing point is situated. Along the mid rib on the dorsal surface, special cup-shaped structure are found called as gemma cups which produce vegetative reproductive structures called gemmae.

The ventral surface of the thallus bears two types of structure – scales and rhizoids. The scales are multicellular arranged in row on each side of mid rib. Scales give protection to thallus. The rhizoids are unicellular, colourless and unbranched that help in fixation and absorption of water and minerals. The thallus is dioecious i.e. Marchantia has different male and female thallus.
Fig 2.5.2 Structure of Marchantia a) Male thallus b) Female thallus Reproduction The reproduction in Marchantia takes place by vegetative and sexual methods.

1. Vegetative Reproduction Vegetative reproduction takes place by various methods. Some methods are described below: a. Fragmentation: The older parts of the thallus decay below the dichotomy and the lobes of thallus are separated from each other. On return of favourable condition these fragments develop into new thalli.

b. Gemma: The most common method of reproduction in Marchantia takes place by special vegetative structures, the gemmae. Gemmae are produced in large number in gemma cup on the dorsal surface of thallus. Each gemma is multicellular, consist of unicellular stalk and multicellular discoid body. It has two notches on the lateral sides. The gemmae also possess mucilage cells, oil cells and rhizoidal cells. The majority of cells of gemma contain chloroplasts except oil cells and rhizoidal cells. The rhizoidal cells give rise to rhizoids. At maturity, the gemma breaks

its connection from the stalk and is carried away by water current, wind or animals. On reaching suitable substratum, each lateral notch gives rise to new thallus. Gemmae present on the male thallus give rise to male plants and those on the female thallus give rise to female plants.
